utterances.text: So we've had about 21.5 thousand felony assaults this year.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Can you provide some raw numbers?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How many of those were domestic violence incidents, attack on government workers, police officers, firefighters, and et cetera?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Just going to go over them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So if you look at police officers and public safety employees combined, that's 10.6% of our felony assaults, or roughly 2,165.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: That's assaults on POs and assaults on public safety workers.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What about the rest, domestic violence or any other?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So domestic violence is 40.7%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: I'm going to get the right numbers right now.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, so about half of a little more than, a little less than half than 21.5.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So it's about like 9,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Yeah, so for DV, our felony assault is 8,275.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: And like I said, 92% arrest rate on that for domestic violence assaults.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: And that's compared to the overall of 20,356 through August.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, what about the rest of the felony assaults?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So about 8.2 thousand domestic violence, about 2.1 thousand government and assaults on police officers.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What about the remainder?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So the remainder are just going to be assault twos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: That's about 14,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: And felony assaults, that's about 14,834.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: That could be if the person's seriously injured, if they're elderly, over 65 years old, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks what has driven the felony assault increase. Gerber explains NYPD is doing its part with 80% arrests but faces recidivism challenges, and notes felony assaults are often one-off incidents that are harder to prevent compared to pattern-based crimes like shootings or burglaries.
chapters.title: Feliz and Gerber on felony assault causes and prevention challenges

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What policing strategies are in place to help bring these numbers down?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And also, what are factors that have led to this increase and have also kept these numbers increasing over these past six years?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So with the felony assaults, like I said, we're driven, this department is data driven, and we're looking to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: We're looking to make arrests on these felony assaults as quickly as possible, and we are doing that at an 80% rate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: That's an all-time high.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: This is, like I said, a direct result of working with the detectives, the police officers on patrol, and identifying the perpetrators and bringing them to custody as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And what would you say has led to this increase, though, and has also allowed these numbers to keep climbing over the years?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No, I think, Chair, I think it's a hard question to answer, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I mean, the PD, as Inspector Howe was describing the data and the arrest data, right, we're doing our part.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We're arresting 80% of felony assault cases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's an incredibly high number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We do have a recidivism issue, as the inspector discussed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that does present a real challenge for us, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I mean, you can imagine the frustration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We go and arrest someone for felony assault.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They're back out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They do it again, second time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They do it a third time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And there are other actors in the criminal justice system and a little broader whole of government perspective on this, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There's in terms of the prosecutors and the judges and the part that they play in this process, obviously a critical role.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There's a whole government question in terms of before that person goes and commits a felony assault, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, how did they get to that point?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, again, other city agencies and other offices that sort of address those types of issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, we, like I said, the PD is doing its part.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I also will point out that, you know, felony assault presents particular challenges from a prevention perspective, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So if you think about, think about shootings, think about murders, think about burglary or robbery patterns, think about GLA patterns through crew activity, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We identify those patterns, we put the cops in the right places, that can have a tremendous prevention effect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Felony assaults often are quite different, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They're often one-offs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It can be, you know, there's a dispute that escalates, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It starts as a verbal dispute, it gets physical, now there's a serious physical injury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We're talking about an assault too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: someone's having an encounter with a police officer and all of a sudden, you know, that person is hitting a cop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The person's, someone's on the train and for whatever reason they're getting hostility with an MTA worker and now they're assaulting an MTA worker, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we investigate those very aggressively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I've had a lot of success in solving those crimes, as the inspector said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But from a prevention perspective,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That is much more challenging when it comes to felony assaults.

chapters.summary: Feliz raises grand larceny auto more than doubling from 3,623 in 2019 to 8,524 this year. Hout notes GLA is down 12.8% this year, highlights Bronx proximity to NJ and Westchester, and describes Operation Pit Crew takedown of 16 people charged with 971 counts.
chapters.title: Feliz asks about grand larceny auto increase vs pre-pandemic

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, so I know my colleagues have questions, so I'll ask one more line of questions, and then I'll pass it on to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So another area of crime that seems to require attention is the grand larceny involving a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They have more than doubled compared to the pre-COVID years, 2019.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Specifically, in 2019, year to date, we had...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This year we've had 8,524.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: That's an increase of over approximately 140%.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Grand loss involving a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What factors have led to this increase?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So when we look at grand larceny auto, just this year we're actually down 12.8% and three out of the five boroughs are down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Grand larcenies are down in the Bronx 29.2% and the Bronx North 26.8%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So when we look at the Bronx for grand larceny, I'll use this as an example, the Bronx,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: has many unique challenges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: It's very close to New Jersey, it's very close to Westchester, and due to that proximity, many stolen vehicles occur outside New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Since 2025, approximately 422 Bronx Grand Largenautos have been recovered outside New York City, and 33% of citywide Grand Largenautos have been recovered in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So it's all about...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Coordination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: We're using our new borough-based order law enforcement teams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: They patrol, they deploy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: They're looking at the data, they're looking at precision, what makes and what models, and if there's any clusters, they're working with the manufacturers, and it shows.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: In 2026, Operation Pit Crew was a vehicle takedown.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: 16 people were charged with 971 counts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: These defendants stole more than $1 million in auto parts, victimizing 252 hard workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So the work shows the crime is trending in the right direction, and they're out there doing the job they need to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Like I said, auto theft is a very complex crime.

chapters.summary: Gerber attributes the GLA spike partly to key fob technology making certain cars easier to steal, notes NYPD has met with car manufacturers about design issues, and discusses working with DAs on pattern cases. Feliz asks whether mopeds are counted as vehicles—NYPD agrees to provide breakdown data.
chapters.title: Gerber on GLA factors, key fob technology, and moped theft classification

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Right, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And I took a hard look at all the numbers, and one thing that I saw was that generally crime doesn't drastically decrease from a year to the next.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Generally, it's progressive, decreases year after year.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So that's something that I kind of noticed for almost every crime.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Obviously, there's a few exceptions, but that's been the general trend.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But I guess the big question is, hoping to compare today's numbers to the numbers from pre-COVID, 2019, when we were pretty safe on that specific issue.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So what would you say has led to that increase?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The numbers have more than doubled, right?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Yes, they have.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What are factors that you would say have played a role in that drastic increase?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, Chair, I think that's a hard question for us to answer, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It goes to a variety of considerations that are actually sort of beyond the PD's purview, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we can...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: can identify the crime trends, and we try to articulate that here today and otherwise, and respond to that, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But in terms of sort of like, what are the underlying causes, for example, of people engaging in felony assaults?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's a very tough question, maybe for anyone to answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's certainly a tough question, you know, for us to answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: To the extent, you know, we see recidivism, again, in the felony assault space, that certainly is a serious consideration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And again, we're doing our part, but there's a limit to what we can do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think on the GLA space, I think one thing, you saw a real spike in GLAs coming out of the pandemic, a tremendous spike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: For the past several years, we've seen decreases, which is really welcome news.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, we've been working a lot with the DAs on these GLA cases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's a very important issue because, you know, these GLAs on a one-off basis, you think about it, oh, it's a property crime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Of course, these crimes can have a dramatic impact on somebody's life, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You have your car stolen, all of a sudden you can't get to work, you can't take your kids to school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we work a lot with the DA's offices, you know, to give them the best possible case that we can, to give them pattern cases when we can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The other issue I just want to flag, a very particular change when it comes to GLAs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think going to your question, we saw and have seen with a number of car types or models problems that make it easier for someone to steal the car, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So certain types of key fobs, I couldn't explain the technology to you, but certain types of key fobs,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: have made it easier for criminals to, through certain technology, steal those cars and steal them very quickly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think that actually contributed to a major spike, or that's certainly one of the causes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I should say, we've actually worked a lot with some of the car manufacturers on this very issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We've had meetings essentially with manufacturers to say, look, hey, there's an issue here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, you designed your car in this way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: This makes it easier for people to steal the car.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's bad for everybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I think we've made some progress on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think that actually is an important consideration here.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And by grand larceny involving a vehicle, does that mean specifically stealing a vehicle, or does that include also the stealing of vehicle parts?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And also, does that include the stealing of a moped?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Is that considered a vehicle for these purposes?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So a two-wheel device, if it's over a certain amount, would be considered a grand larceny auto.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: The parts would be considered a grand larceny.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Do you have a breakdown based on the grand larceny of involving a vehicle numbers, cars versus mopeds?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I've heard a lot of complaints about mopeds being stolen.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So, Chair, we don't have that with us, but I think we have that.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I think that is data we can pull for you, and we will provide it.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, sounds good.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So I have many more questions, but I'll pause here.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know my colleagues have many questions, but just want to say it seems like we've obviously made a lot of progress on shootings, murders, burglaries, robberies, but compared to the numbers from prior to the pandemic, it seems like there's still a lot of room

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: for progress on many crime categories.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Many of these categories seem to be...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Drastically up compared to pre-COVID, including the grand larceny involving auto, felony assaults, and many other crime categories that I'll ask about later.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But for now, I'll pause.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'll pass it to Public Advocate Williams and then Council Members Areola, Nurse, and Hanks.

chapters.summary: Williams acknowledges the pressure NYPD faced during a busy summer with NBA Finals, World Cup, and other events. She praises community affairs and the Office of Community Safety/Crisis Management System, noting some violence interrupters have been harmed.
chapters.title: PA Williams acknowledges summer challenges and community safety partners

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And first, Inspector and Deputy Commissioner, I want to make sure we highlight that this was a very, very busy summer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: You acknowledged that in your testimony, NBA Finals, Knicks in five, the World Cup, sale to 50, everything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: FIFA, everything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I do want to acknowledge the pressure that NYPD was under to make sure all those things move slowly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I think many partners for the past 10, 20 years have put so much effort into dealing with shootings and murders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I just want to acknowledge the difficult job that NYPD has.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I also want to shout out the community affairs who doesn't get the praise they should, having to manage a lot of police and public relations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I do want to make sure we shout out the Office of Community Safety and the Crisis Management System, who are also doing just a dangerous job as well, not the same job

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: in the way you get guns off the street and not answering 911 calls in the way you do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But I want to make sure they get acknowledged, some of them have been harmed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I think that combination has helped.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm frustrated in the newness, I guess, close to 20 years, and I sometimes see the same thing happening over and over, and we're getting similar results.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I think it's great that we are historic loads of murder and shooters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Those are real people, real names.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Sadly, a lot of those victims look like mine, and a lot of their mothers look like mine that are mourning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So this is very, very, very personal to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But I don't want to see continued harms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I'm just trying to see how we continue to do things differently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So you mentioned the crew takedowns.

chapters.summary: Williams asks whether after crew takedowns, NYPD coordinates with other agencies to prevent recurrence. Gerber agrees there's a role for other city agencies after takedowns to help communities reclaim spaces, and says takedowns are not secret to other agencies.
chapters.title: PA Williams on crew takedowns and inter-agency collaboration

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Which I've seen happen now time after time, often in the same spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So this is a great...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We can talk about should they be taken down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Sometimes you do need some of those law enforcement tools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Sometimes they're too much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But if we all agree sometimes that it's needed, after those crew takedowns, are there discussions with other agencies, are there discussions with the Office of Community Safety of what needs to be happening in that community so that you don't have to come back again?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right, so that was a community safety, of course, is brand new.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, you know, I tell you, you're asking about historically, there isn't really a history here, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But I take your point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Well, let me just say this, because I've asked this for the past 16 years, before Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The question was, are you speaking to other agencies?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We have an office now, but there are other agencies that could have always been brought in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: To talk about what is it that we can do here, because the police have done their part, what else can be done to make sure the police don't have to come back again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right, so let me just say, I completely agree with you that we have one of these takedowns, which often are, as you say, geographically concentrated, right, a particular space, you say some violent crew have taken over,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: a playground, a certain block, whatever it may be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We do that takedown, and that then creates an opportunity for the community to take back that space, 100%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And yes, there are other city agencies that have an important role to play in that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, look, when we do these takedowns, it's not a secret.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It is known to everyone involved, known to everyone in the community, known to other city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I think...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I certainly agree with you that when we have a crew takedown of whatever sort, I think there's a role for other city agencies to play, particularly in that moment, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's a very particular moment, okay, when, you know, shooters have been taken off the street, drug dealers taken off the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: How can, again, the whole government approach, how can agencies help people in that community take back that space for themselves, for their kids?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So I agree with you on that completely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I just, I don't think that it's, again, it's not a secret when we do these things, and I think there is an opportunity for other city agencies to play a very important role.

chapters.summary: Williams pushes NYPD to proactively lead collaborative conversations with other agencies, noting the same neighborhoods need both law enforcement and social services. She urges sharing CompStat data with other agencies and asks about response time delays where complainants leave before police arrive.
chapters.title: PA Williams pushes NYPD to lead collaborative efforts and asks about response times

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So, again, running out, so I'm going to push a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But $60 billion in NYPD, right, has a very large voice in the public safety space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So being pushed, or this being pushed by NYPD, I think would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I do want to just push the Mumdani administration as a whole to force these conversations to occur that should have happened very naturally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I would say not just in the takedowns, but when a shooting occurs, when North Bronx

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: sees a type of violence increase that we've seen, what are the conversations that are happening between PD and Office of Community Safety before the takedown so that all the resources are going there?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I've been saying this for I don't know how long.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It's the same map.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So wherever we're sending the law enforcement, we could be sending so many other resources, and we should be doing it collaboratively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I've seen this happen in other...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: the counties and other cities that actually are working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The best places I've seen them are where there is not tension between those things, not tension between the top departments, and folks are working collaboratively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we've erased that tension, so I'm hoping we can continue to do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we're sharing in CompStat meetings with other agencies that we should be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I just want to push for this collaborative effort because the more we keep asking or relying on PD, the more we're going to have the type of issues that we don't want to see here and everybody wants us to be safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So my message is, please, there are things that we've been talking for so long.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This administration has done a lot, and I'm very happy about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But there's collaborations and pushed conversations that we should be having that we're not.

chapters.summary: Williams asks whether NYPD reports when complainants are gone upon police arrival and whether crime data is updated after audits. Gerber says they'll try to pull data on complainant absence and confirms crime numbers are always updated with latest classifications.
chapters.title: PA Williams on response time data and crime data revision updates

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: If I could just ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I had one question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I know that response times have become delayed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I experienced it myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I also sometimes do that delay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Complaintants are gone when law enforcement comes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I just want to know if we have any numbers on times that police may have arrived and the complaint wasn't there because that wouldn't show up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And also, in my report, I had a kind of question of when you give the numbers and there's an audit and there's a change, are those reports?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Changed after.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yeah, so sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So first on the question about, you know, when you have a police response and the complainant is no longer there, you know, I just don't know if we have data on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If we do, we will.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: provide it to you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I have to look at sort of how we track that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But certainly if we can pull that data, we will provide it to your office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: With regard to the crime data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So when a crime gets reclassified, the numbers get updated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right, so what we're putting out, however we're putting out, whether it's Comstat 2.0 online, when we're providing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: our monthly data to the state, which goes to the feds as well, when we're putting out the monthly press releases, whatever form we're doing this,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We're always using the latest numbers that we have, reflecting, as you know, changes that happen in crime classification in the normal course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so, yes, the numbers do reflect that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: New Yorkers don't feel as safe as we actually are, and we've got to figure out why that is, and we've got to make sure they can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Have faith in the numbers that are being pushed out there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I really appreciate this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, public advocate.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I want to recognize Councilmember Murano.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And next, we'll hear from Councilmember Ariola.

chapters.summary: Ariola highlights that 263 individuals have been arrested three or more times for felony assault, up 205% from 2018. Gerber confirms the number and calls it frustrating, noting NYPD is only one piece of the criminal justice system.
chapters.title: CM Ariola questions NYPD on repeat felony assault offenders

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I will say that I was very encouraged by the takedowns of the crews in the areas.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I want to just state that that is why it is very important that we maintain the gang database.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We hear a great deal about

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Overall crime being down, but the NYPD's own figures show arrests of people with at least three prior felony assault arrests have risen 206% since 2018, from 86 people to 263 people.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Is that an accurate number?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So this year, we've had 263 individuals that have been arrested three or more times for felony assault, and that's up 205% compared to 2018.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And yes, that's three or more arrests this year.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So what does that statistic tell you about the condition of our criminal justice system?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It is frustrating, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I think, again, we are one piece of the criminal justice system, but only one piece.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And there's a limit to what we can do, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If we make the arrest and we present a good case, you know, there are other actors in the system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Obviously, every case has to be evaluated on its own terms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But it definitely, I think, as a descriptive matter, it is a problem.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It's a problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It is a problem if we are over and over.

chapters.summary: Ariola raises videos of officers refusing to take crime reports, including a Washington Square Park incident. Gerber calls the video unacceptable, confirms IAB investigation, and says most officers take reports properly but misconduct is disciplined severely under Commissioner Tisch.
chapters.title: CM Ariola on crime reporting refusals and Washington Square Park video

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Do you know how many additional New Yorkers were assaulted this year by defendants who had already been arrested for another violent offense while a previous case of theirs was still pending?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we will pull that for you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I don't think we have it here, but that is data that we have and we can provide.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So I just want to talk now about reporting of crimes.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We've all seen the videos circulating online most recently from officers in Washington Square Park and heard that several reports from Times Square or elsewhere in the city of officers either refusing to take a report or...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Dissuading individuals from filing reports.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Do you ever receive complaints from the public about officers refusing to take a report or misclassifying what they say?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yeah, so first of all, I just want to say that with that video, I'm familiar with the video, totally unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It is under investigation by IAB, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have that case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's under investigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And yes, this is not a new issue, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Most officers do this the right way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I want to say it's actually very important, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Most cops are taking crime reports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They're there to help victims.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They're trying to achieve justice for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You're going to have a small number of officers who don't do this the right way, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There are times when that's negligence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: lack of training, a training issue, and there are times when it's misconduct.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I want to be very clear that when we have misconduct, particularly under Commissioner Tisch, these matters are investigated rigorously and the disciplinary consequences can be severe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I also, if I may, I just want to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There are many reasons why it's so problematic, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The obvious reason is just terribly wrong, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Someone experienced a crime, they're trying to report it, and officers not taking their complaint, and in that case, apparently almost seeming to mock it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's just wrong, full stop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It undermines credibility of the public, which is a terrible thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There's also another issue, which is the department, like everything we've been talking about, it runs, the department runs on crime data, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we need good data for deployment, for resource allocation, for follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so I'm going to stop you there because I have a couple more questions.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks about 911 call-to-report audits and the 580 officer budget cut. Gerber describes ICAT audits comparing 911 calls to complaint reports, and says while more officers are always preferable, NYPD is having tremendous success with current staffing.
chapters.title: CM Ariola on 911 audit system and 580 officer budget cut

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So because we're on crime data and statistics and follow-up, does the NYPD keep a record of 911 calls for crimes being reported compared to the amount of reports that are actually being taken by the officers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right, so we actually do audits on this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we have, as part of our auditing system, and we can talk more about that, but one of the audits that we do...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Is an ICAT audit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: What we will do is, and we do this both at the command level in terms of self-inspections, and then separately from the crime audit team, we'll do ICAT audits, where we take 911 calls,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And radio runs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we have a sampling of how we do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then we check.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we say, okay, there was a call for burglary in progress.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: A robbery in progress.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Okay, now we're going to check.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: One, was a complaint taken?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And two, if it was taken, was it taken properly?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we do have a whole auditing process in place to address this issue.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: May I ask just a little lead time?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So in this year's budget, Mayor Momdani cut 580 police officers from the budget.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Do you have any idea where those police officers might have been assigned if they had been budgeted?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And do you believe those additional officers, specifically the ones that may have been assigned to the Bronx, would have had a beneficial impact on crime stats in that borough?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So I certainly can't speak to where sort of hypothetically officers would have been assigned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And, you know, look, obviously, if we didn't have budgetary restrictions, like in a vacuum, as between more police officers and fewer police officers, of course we're always going to want more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But, but.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It makes sense that if we had those extra 580 cops, we would.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: have 580 cops more on the street and less crime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But I do want to say that we understand, obviously, that we have budgetary constraints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we feel like with the cops that we have, we're having a tremendous amount of success in fighting crime.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks whether juvenile crimes are included in statistics (Gerber confirms yes) and whether crimes are being downgraded from felonies to lesser charges. Gerber acknowledges this sometimes happens through training issues, sloppiness, or misconduct, with extensive auditing systems in place.
chapters.title: CM Ariola on juvenile crime stats and crime downgrading concerns

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And we also have had a high incidence of minors committing crimes in our communities because they are underage.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: If they get caught and they're released to their parent, there are no consequences.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Do those crimes get added to the statistics?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yeah, any, any, Council Member, is the question?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Is the question whether crimes committed by juveniles are part of our crime statistics?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, just final.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Are you aware of any crimes that are being broken down to decrease to more serious crime stats to less serious crime stats?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Like, for example, a felony burglary might be broken down to a trespass or a petty larceny.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Are you aware of that taking place at all?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: When arrests are being made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Does that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yes, there are times when that happens, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I mean, sorry, just to go back to the whole sort of process that we have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Crime classifications, first of all, again, can change the normal course for all sorts of reasons, and you would expect them to change at times for totally normal reasons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There are times when the cops get it wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It does happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And again, that can be through sometimes a training issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It can be through sloppiness, and every once in a while it can be misconduct.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That does happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Lots and lots and lots of checks in place, an incredibly, I would say, exhaustive auditing system with a disciplinary component to get at these sorts of issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we have been particularly vigilant about this under Police Commissioner Tisch.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So does that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yes, there are times when that happens, and we have a lot of systems in place to catch it and fix it, and when discipline is warranted, to impose discipline.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you for the extra time, Chair.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks what percentage of felony assaults involve repeat offenders—Hout says approximately 20% are by those arrested two or more times. Feliz then asks for per-borough officer counts; Hout provides breakdowns showing roughly equal deployment across boroughs.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz on repeat offender percentage and per-borough officer counts

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Councilmember Nurse, but briefly.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So you mentioned that repeat offenders have played a big role with relation to the numbers related to felony assaults.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: About what percent of felony assaults would you say are due to repeat offenders?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Sorry, just one second, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I want to give you that answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So those arrested two or more times is approximately 20% of our felony assaults.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: 20% of the felony assaults are individuals arrested two more times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And also, we've been talking a lot about Bronx and cop count.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: About how many police officers do we have per borough?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Could you give us a breakdown of that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So 1,257 in Manhattan South.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: 1,573 in Manhattan North, 1,722 in the Bronx South, 1,791 in the Bronx North, 1,224 in Queens South, 1,259 in Queens North,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Brooklyn North, 1,791.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Bronx North, 1,259.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Bronx South, 1,361.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Queens South, 1,122.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Staten Island, 543.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz

chapters.summary: Feliz notes 40% of city murders and shootings are in the Bronx despite roughly equal officer counts, arguing more police are needed there. Gerber says Bronx is leading the city in crime reduction, additional mobile field forces are deployed as needed, and the 580 cut officers were never banked on.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz on Bronx resource allocation and need for 580 additional officers

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, in the Bronx, again, if my math is correct, 40% of the murders that this city has seen this year have been in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: About 40% of the shooting incidents and shooting victims that the city has seen this year also in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So what explains that?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Division of resources.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And it seems like we also need to, obviously public safety is a shared responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: There's a lot of factors that play a role.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Obviously we need good schools, opportunity, good jobs, but it seems like we need more police in the Bronx based on the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I mean, Chair, I would say, first of all, as you know, overall Bronx is leading the city in crime reductions, which is welcome news.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: To your point, right, in terms of murders and shootings in the Bronx, these are the numbers, right, assigned to the borough commands.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: When you have a spike in shootings, right, we are going to send in more cops, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's not accounted for here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, for example, you have a spike in shootings in a precinct, we're going to be sending mobile field forces there, sending specialty teams there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that's sort of the precision policing and deployment that we talked about earlier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's not just these resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We will move resources across the city, right, as necessary to address changing crime conditions.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Based on the historical issues that the Bronx has had related to crime, on average, though, how many police officers would you say we have, including those assigned, but also those additional resources?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: On average.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's a question we can answer right here, right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We can try to, we can do some math.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And again, and Chair, just to be clear, the reason why it's a hard question to answer is that it literally changes by the day, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You could have a mobile field force over here one day and over there a different day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that's true for special teams as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, I mean, it's going to involve some math and some analysis, but I think we can try to come up with some sort of approximation for you and get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, sounds good.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And I think, you know, obviously, again, public safety is a shared responsibility, but police officers play a big role.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This might support the argument that we need those 580 additional cops, that new class that was canceled right before we...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Voted for the budget.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So we'll next hear from Councilmember Nurse, then Hanks, then Caban, and then Long and then Morano.

chapters.summary: Nurse cites Gothamist reporting nearly 100,000 civil summonses last fiscal year with nearly half dismissed. Gerber shares frustration, noting dismissals are due to paperwork issues not improper issuance, and that officers choose civil over criminal summonses in most cases.
chapters.title: CM Nurse on civil summons dismissal rates

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I think I just have three questions.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Gothamist reported this week that the NYPD issued almost 100,000 civil summons last fiscal year, and nearly half of which were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And given such a high dismissal rate, do you think

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We should be reallocating resources to more serious crime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: First of all, we share the frustration in terms of what's being described in that article.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We're not happy about that for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I do want to emphasize, and consistent with the article, they're being dismissed not because they were improperly issued, the paperwork's not being done properly, it's not being filled out properly, handwriting issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We need to fix that.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're saying that the issue is that people are not, their handwriting is bad?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If you read the article, the article describes how in some cases, you know, when the officer is filling it out, in some cases it's not filling it out properly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In some cases, the way it's described from Oath and the article, it's like that they couldn't see what was being sort of handwritten on the summons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we need to work on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The officers do get training in the academy on how to properly fill out the oath.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Understood, understood.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Just because of time, I don't mean to be rude.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: But, I mean, so some of them are getting dismissed because of paper.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: The way you're filling it out.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: But, you know, back to the point, do you think that given so many of them are being dismissed, maybe you should reallocate some of those resources to more serious violent crime?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So again, but they're not being dismissed because of the underlying issue, but to your question,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: in many situations, actually in most of these situations, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: all but most, an officer is in a situation where the officer could give an oath summons or give a criminal summons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Most things that are oath summons eligible are also criminal summons eligible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so in these cases, you know, an officer is saying, you know, the officer is choosing not to give a criminal summons, not to go down the criminal path.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: When he or she could, and say, no, I'm going to do this through the civil process, without any prospect of criminal sanction.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, I understand, and I understand the discretion being offered.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I still think it's a pretty high dismissal rate.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Since you brought up criminal summons, you all are also issuing a lot of criminal summons.

chapters.summary: Nurse raises Vital City data showing criminal summonses at an eight-year high with nearly 60,000, driven by transit rule violations. Gerber explains 90% of transit summonses are civil TAB summonses, with criminal summonses reserved for recidivists with three or more prior TABs.
chapters.title: CM Nurse on criminal summonses and transit rule enforcement

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Vital City reported that criminal summons in the first half of 2026 reached an eight-year high with nearly 60,000 summons.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: From what I'm understanding is being driven mostly by the increase in enforcement of transit rule violations, things like disobeying subway signs or taking up more than one seat on the subway.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: You know, again, like, why are we spending so many resources on that versus serious crime?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, so you have officers in transit, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And they're seeing, they're doing their work, and they're seeing someone who is in violation of the transit rules, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, that could give rise, often the answer, by the way, is they do not, there's disobeying subway signs or taking up more than one seat on the subway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They correct the issue and that's that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: When it comes to enforcement, they have the option in every case that you could give a tab summons or a criminal summons.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: You know, again, like, why are we spending so many resources on that versus serious crime?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: As a matter of law, every trans-able violation is criminal summons eligible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You have officers in transit, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And they're seeing, they're doing their work, and they're seeing someone who is in violation of the transit rules, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In that universe of summonses in transit, 90% of the time, it's TAP, not criminal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, that could give rise, often the answer, by the way, is they do not, there's disobeying subway signs or taking up more than one seat on the subway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So in the vast majority of situations, as between a TAP summons and a criminal summons, an officer is saying, no, I'm going to go the civil route, not the criminal route.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There's disobeying subway signs or taking up more than one seat on the subway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Where you do see the criminal summonses,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: in transit, when you have a tab recidivist, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Someone who received three or more tabs in the last two years, or has three or more unanswered or unpaid tabs in the last eight years, and in that relatively narrow class of cases, when tabs have been repeatedly given, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And now, because of the person to tab recidivist, okay, now is the criminal summons route.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But again, 90% of the time, civil summons is not criminal.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It would be great to get in the follow-up of that nearly 60,000 criminal summonses.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: What are we looking at?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: From my understanding, I hear what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Someone on the train is issuing, okay, they're going to go the other route and not a criminal, but who are we issuing these criminal summonses to if they're recidivists?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Are they people who are homeless?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I mean, like, who's on there, you know, taking out their...

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: more than one seat, you know, that you are now getting a criminal summons to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Just to be clear, when I say recidivist, I mean, we have a particular policy, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So it'll say in our system, this person has gotten three or more tabs in the last two years or has three or more unpaid answer tabs in the last eight years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It is not based on whether the person is homeless or not at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In a situation in which, okay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I think it would just be helpful if you could send some of that, a breakdown of some of that in the follow-up, and we can write out a proper question for you.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: My last question is on unconstitutional policing.

chapters.summary: Nurse cites the federal monitor finding NYPD still engaging in unconstitutional stops 13 years after Floyd v. NYC. Gerber says unconstitutional stops are constitutional violations not crimes, confirms officers have been disciplined but none fired, and says compliance rates are above 90% for patrol officers.
chapters.title: CM Nurse on unconstitutional stops and officer discipline

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Last month, the federal monitor overseeing the police department in the Floyd stop and frisk litigation found that 13 years since the federal court

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: found the NYPD stop and frisk program to be unconstitutional, the department is still routinely engaging in unconstitutional stops, frisks, and other acts.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: The department's position, this is a question, is that unconstitutional policing or illegal policing is a crime, correct?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I'm not sure I have a question.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: My question is, do you believe that unconstitutional policing is a crime?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If to the extent a stop violates the Fourth Amendment, that is a constitutional violation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Is that a crime?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's a constitutional violation, which is significant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But is that a crime?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So what would you call it then?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: A constitutional violation.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So what, what, how many

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Officers have been fired or disciplined for engaging in illegal policing or unconstitutional stops.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Let's just say in the last few years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we can, I mean, I don't have the data here, but we can certainly get you data on discipline issued in connection with bad stops, frisk, or searches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I do want to emphasize something.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Well, so can you do off the top of your head just this year?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Have there been any disciplinary actions?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Has anybody been fired for an unconstitutional stop?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Fired for an unconstitutional stop?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Have officers received discipline?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The answer to that question is yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sheriff, if I may just have a moment to just fully respond to the question, please.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: What the monitors report say is that actually the vast majority of officers in the department are doing this constitutionally the right way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If you look at the data in those reports, in terms of certainly in the patrol response, 911 responses, complainant victim responses, the compliance rates are incredibly high.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: What are the compliance rates?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In many cases, you're north of 90%.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And they're very, very high.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So we still have a little bit more to go.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So I guess what I'm saying is, like, what are the concrete actions that you all are doing to address that remaining group of folks that are not being compliant?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yeah, and again, I'm talking about the patrol officers, not the specialty teams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But we are working every day with the monitor on this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And for example, like what we're doing in compliance that we're doing with compliance reviews, the work that we're doing, I literally like every day we are working on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And working very closely with the monitors team because while we've made a tremendous amount of progress and as you know as you know the number of stops that the department conducts has fallen over 90 percent

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: uh since since let's say 20 you know 2011 2012 right over 90 percent

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: the nature of policing in the city has changed dramatically fair enough but i guess my point still stands you know what exactly are you doing

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: what are the how many you know in the follow-up if you could provide i understand you're not prepared to talk about that today fine in the follow-up if you could provide you know what are the concrete actions you're taking for that remaining

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: percentage to get us to 100%, which should be the goal.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: What are the disciplinary actions that have been taken?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It sounds like no one's been fired, even though this has been something for 13 years.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So we'd love to just get more of a breakdown.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Nurse.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
