utterances.text: And by the way, we're going to do a second round, so if there's any data that you don't have right now, feel free to ask about it on the second round.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Hopefully, you're able to look at your documents and get the information.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Councilmember Hanks and then Caban.

chapters.summary: Hanks notes the 121st precinct in Staten Island has major crime up 1.5% and felony assaults up 25.1%, asking what triggers additional deployment. Hout explains the CompStat process of bringing stakeholders together to analyze data and deploy resources.
chapters.title: CM Hanks on Staten Island 121st precinct crime increase and deployment

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you so much for coming.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: We always appreciate the hard work of the...

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So I'd like to kind of circle back where it comes to the precision policing.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Of course, citywide, you know, major crime is down, but the picture is really not the same everywhere.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So in the 121st precinct in Staten Island, major crime is up 1.5% and felony assaults are up 25.1%.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Comstat should help NYPD seeing where a problem is growing and respond quickly.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So basically my question is with numbers like this, what has to happen before NYPD sends more officers?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: You know, when NYPD sees a crime category increase in a precinct, how does it relegate their deployment, and how do we work with addressing problems

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: with a scalpel?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So anytime there's a shooting or a crime spike throughout the department, whether it be Staten Island or the Bronx or wherever, we come together as a department and we look at the data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: And we see where we need more resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So with that, the posture of the department, you know, we see a string of shootings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: When we analyze, we respond, we deploy accordingly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: You know, we would talk about something like this at a comp stat meeting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: We'd bring all the stakeholders together, meaning the precinct CO would be there, the intelligence bureau would be there, the detective bureau would be there, and we would share ideas and we would share our vision.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: in that area and see what we could do better and where we can improve.

chapters.summary: Hanks raises a September 14 incident where a loaded gun was found in a student's backpack at Curtis High School. Hout describes youth violence zones focused on schools, routes, and transit, with precinct commanders meeting weekly with principals and a juvenile desk for field guidance.
chapters.title: CM Hanks on loaded gun found at Curtis High School

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So in that same line, on September 14th, school safety agents discovered a loaded gun from the backpack of an 18-year-old student at Curtis High School after breaking up a fight.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thankfully, no one was hurt, but a loaded weapon in school in the 120th precinct raises serious concerns about student safety and how young people are getting access to weapons.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So after an incident like this,

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: What does NYPD do to find out where the gun came from, how the student got it, whether other young people or weapons may be involved?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Right, so a gun in a school is very serious, and we take it that way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So when we look at it, youth violence in general,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: We deploy, the department has implemented youth violence zones, and they're modeled after a data-driven strategy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So these zones are focused on areas where young people are most at risk, and that includes the school, and that also includes around the school and the routes to the school, major commuter corridors, major bus stops.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: And it's not just we can't do it alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: It's coordination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So every precinct CO is talking to the principal weekly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: We're working with the schools, working with the school safety, with the parents, with the students, with the transit bureau, because many kids use transit to get home on a bus or a train.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: My office, the Office of Crime Control Strategies, has a juvenile desk where officers from the field can call and get guidance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: And we've made great strides with that desk.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And Chair, may I have one more question, please?

chapters.summary: Hanks asks whether NYPD shares CompStat data with violence interrupters and nonprofit partners. Hout says precinct commanding officers share information with schools, school safety agents, and various partners, with detailed plans for youth violence corridors.
chapters.title: CM Hanks on sharing CompStat data with violence interrupters

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So that now leads me to my next question.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Comstat helps NYPD see crime increasing.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: It's not clear whether NYPD shares the information with our violence interrupters or other nonprofit public safety partners.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So, and I think that that was part of your answer to my second question.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I think that we just kind of need to expand on how NYPD shares that information and what do partners receive and how quickly so we can work as a community together to make sure that everyone is safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So we share that information, like I said, with many different partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Each precinct, you know, the CEO has got to have a detailed plan involved in regards to youth violence in school corridors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: And we do share that information with the school and with the school safety agents.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks why a GLA crew takedown took over a year despite daily complaints of cars on blocks without wheels. Gerber explains building strong conspiracy cases takes time, connecting incidents and participants, and that crews act quickly making investigation challenging.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz on GLA takedown timeline and resource questions

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Councilor McCowan.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But briefly, I just want to say again that we appreciate the NYPD's focus on focusing on the worst crimes, murders, and shootings.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I think the focus on that has been able to bring the numbers to the lowest numbers ever.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But I guess my question on that is,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Are there any obstacles that we've seen on the issue of felony assaults and also grand larceny of auto?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Is resources an issue?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I mean, for example, you know, last year there was a recent takedown of the group, but for over a year, I remember in the Bronx and throughout the, they eventually did another part of the city,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: every single day I would receive, I'm not exaggerating, every single day I would receive at least three to four new pictures of incidents of basically cars on the floor.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: No wheels, no rims.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And, you know, of course, resources are not unlimited, but I'm wondering why would it take so long to hold this group accountable?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: To my knowledge, they were doing it for over a year.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Is it a lack of resources?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Obviously, you can't focus on everything at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Is resources an issue?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Well, but I mean, part of it is we also want to build a strong case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And there's always, there are trade-offs here, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You want to act quickly for obvious reasons, but you want to have a strong case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You want to make sure that the case is going to hold up in court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Doing that takes time, particularly in conspiracy cases, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And you're just, it's not a one-off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You're connecting various incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: connecting various participants in, let's say, a GLA crew.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then part of it is also in the nature of the crime, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You have situations where, you know, it's in the middle of the night.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: My understanding is some of these crews are able to do this remarkably quickly, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so they're, you know,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: By the time someone even realizes the crime has occurred, they are long gone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so that presents investigative challenges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The case we were talking about is a great case and a product of tremendous work by the Detective Bureau.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And it has had a tremendous effect in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But in order to have that effect, to bring the successful case, it does take time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Councilmember Caban, then Wong, and then Marano.

chapters.summary: Cabán challenges the premise that more police means less crime, cites GIV community reductions, and criticizes NYPD for not acknowledging community partners until prompted by the Public Advocate. She also questions the reasoning behind targeting homeless people as transit summons recidivists.
chapters.title: CM Cabán on summonses, community partners, and recidivism framing

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Gerber, I'm going to start with a statement.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I promise I will give a cue for when I'm asking you a question.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm going to start with my colleague mentioning the summonses.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I just want to state, to kind of add context to the record, that a lot of these summonses are being dismissed because they are legally facially insufficient.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It's not just some, like, sloppy handwriting, and maybe we shouldn't be wasting time on those things.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I think there also was a suggestion that more...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Police officers would mean less crime and actually there is a really sound assessment that more police officers are not

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: needed to reduce crime.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And that's a trend that is seen locally, statewide, and nationally.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It's backed up by data.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: In fact, Governor Hochul specifically points out that the murder rates in GIV communities have huge decreases.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And so that is a state program that uses community-based orgs working with police to intercede before violence happens.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And so here in New York City, we have something better.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We have CMS that we know from the Comptroller's report could use some strengthening, whether it's the bureaucratic hurdles, some of the oversight hurdles, some of the funding mandates.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I thought it was curious that it wasn't until the public advocate brought up crisis.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Violence interrupters that it was acknowledged that those are partners in the work.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: When you guys were asked, hey, how are you getting these numbers down?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: You said DAs and police and precision policing, but you did not offer community partners up once in that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It had to be brought up by the public advocate, and I think that that's telling.

chapters.summary: Cabán asks whether NYPD reports unconstitutional stops the same way as crime statistics. Gerber says the monitor publishes regular reports with stop data, but Cabán presses for a direct yes or no on whether NYPD itself reports unconstitutional stops publicly.
chapters.title: CM Cabán presses on reporting of unconstitutional stops

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I want to also address recidivism.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I mean, the idea that you're not targeting homeless people for being recidivists when the place that they sleep is on the train and therefore they would likely be recidivists.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Again, I just...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I don't understand or don't buy the reasoning behind that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But I do want to ask you, and I ask you now, Councilmember Nurse asked about the constitutional stops.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: No, they're not crimes.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: but they're violations of our constitutional rights.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Are those constitutional stops reported, unconstitutional stops reported in the same way that crime statistics are reported?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Do you report on unconstitutional stops?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So I'm not sure I totally understand the question, but...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Do you report on unconstitutional stops?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: You're saying that 90% of stops are good, but are you reporting when unconstitutional stops are made the same way you report when a crime is recorded?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Do you report unconstitutional stops?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So what you actually have, right, as you know, is the monitor puts out regular reports that has all sorts of data broken down in various ways about unconstitutional stops identified, frankly identified, not only by the monitor.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: No, the monitor.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Does NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Council member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Does NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Report in the same way they do crime statistics, unconstitutional stops.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: What we do, right, is we actually have an incredibly extensive auditing system to catch bad stops for instant searches, which the monitors reports,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: as you know, which as you know, the monitor says, as you know, the monitor has said repeatedly, those are very much in line with the monitor analyses, and that is actually included in regular reports to the public from the monitor.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We'll give both of you extra time.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So, yeah, if you're going to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It would be nice just to get direct answers to my questions.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Now,

chapters.summary: Cabán asks whether policing can solve recidivism, noting repeated felony assault arrests suggest it cannot. Gerber agrees there are root causes—economic and educational disparities—beyond NYPD's charge, and that other system actors and agencies play critical roles.
chapters.title: CM Cabán on recidivism and limits of policing for root causes

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: You mentioned the example of a person who gets arrested for felony assault one, two, three times.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Have you thought about maybe the fact that policing and the criminal legal system isn't equipped to and can't solve that problem then?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Has that occurred to you guys?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: To the extent your question is, should we go out and arrest someone who committed a felony?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's not my question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I 100% agree that we are doing our part, and there are other actors out there in the system, very broadly conceived.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Gerber, that's not my question.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm just saying, do you agree that it's possible that the job that you were tasked to do as NYPD to make these arrests and pass off to the DA, that that alone...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Cannot solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: What that does is hold someone accountable for a particular crime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If your point is that we are doing our part and other parts of the system are failing, that I agree with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But to the extent the question is, are we doing our part to hold someone accountable for a felony?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That wasn't my question.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: My question is whether it solves the problem of the recidivist act.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And so I think the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So now my next question is, what are the underlying factors of instability that could be causing multiple bouts of

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: assault, for example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And Councilmember, to the extent your point, which I understand is, there are

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: underlying social issues that go far beyond anything the NYPD can deal with in terms of economic disparities, for example, or educational disparities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Councilmember, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There are root causes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There are root causes of these problems that the NYPD is not charged with addressing.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We're allowed to agree on things.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It didn't have to be that difficult.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So I want to move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you for the additional time.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Yeah, you can take another minute.

chapters.summary: Cabán asks whether police violence is counted in crime statistics. Gerber says if an officer commits a crime it's included, but justified use of force is not. Cabán argues excessive force settlements show a gap in crime data, noting police account for up to 5% of U.S. murders.
chapters.title: CM Cabán on police violence exclusion from crime statistics

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Now, is police violence counted in your crime statistics?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: What do you mean by police violence?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Well, when a police officer commits an assault on the job.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Is that included in the crime statistics that the NYPD puts out?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If you're talking about a police officer who goes and commits a crime, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If a police officer goes, commits a crime for which a person will be arrested and prosecuted, would that go into our statistics?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: When officers, as they sometimes have to do, unfortunately, use force in connection with policing, and that is at times necessary and appropriate, consistent with the law and consistent with our policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No, of course that would not count.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Does it get included in the crime statistics when they use excessive force?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If an officer has committed a crime, if we have a member of service, like anyone else in the city, who commits a crime, that will be included in the crime data.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So it shows a gap, right?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Because we're seeing, and we still see them in the millions and millions of dollars of settlements we get because of instances of police brutality, of excessive force, that no, those officers aren't being charged with a crime.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: If they were in civilian clothing, they probably would be.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Let me finish.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And so there might be a settlement saying, this officer, this officer.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Used excessive force.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Outside of this context, that would be a crime, but it's not included in the crime statistics.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So I guess what I'm saying is that the crime statistics don't really show the full picture of what we're looking at, and I would hope that we start

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: using a metric of data that is a little bit more comprehensive than that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: For example, police are responsible for up to 5% of murders in the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: That's not captured in crime statistics, right?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I would like to know if the crime statistics also are, are they measuring other

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: parts of public safety, like do our crime statistics measure how many people die because they're sleeping out in the cold?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Councilmember, our crime statistics, it will not surprise you to learn, measure crime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There are many other important data sets out there in statistics that are not measured through NYPD crime data.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So our crime statistics and, listen.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Indulge me in this exercise.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Our crime statistics also don't reflect the number of people who die because they didn't get medical care, mental health care, etc.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It doesn't account for people who die or left unsafe because of workplace conditions, anything like that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It doesn't.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It just is.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Our crime data reflects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Crime complaints in the city.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So do you think...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That we're measuring.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Do you think it's a good and accurate measure of the overall safety of our city, our crime statistics?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think it is a very good measure, an outstanding measure of crime in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, there are many other things that are incredibly important and significant and need to be measured, but they're not measured through NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Crime statistics.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Listen, I just want to get that on the record.

chapters.summary: Cabán asks whether crime statistics measure overall city safety including deaths from lack of healthcare, housing, or workplace conditions. Gerber says crime data measures crime complaints only. Cabán asks whether NYPD advocates for investments in other agencies; Gerber says NYPD does not weigh in on other agencies' budgets.
chapters.title: CM Cabán on comprehensive safety metrics and NYPD advocacy for other agencies

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Now, I guess to wrap this up and sort of bring it together.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We'll have a second round.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'd like to just wrap up by saying thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Would you then, if your mission is public safety, right, are you guys in the practice of going to other agencies or going to the mayor and saying, hey, we would like to see investments in

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: housing, IMT teams, fact teams, or whatever, because that'll help us do our jobs.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Is that happening?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Councilmember, we certainly, to the extent the question is, do we want to see public safety writ large in every respect in New York City improved?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The answer is, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Are we sort of weighing in on other agencies'budgets?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No, we're not doing that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: If you want to see it safer and you agree that these other strategies would be helpful, why wouldn't you go to an agency partner and say, hey, we're going to lobby on your behalf.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We want you to bolster up because it would make our officers safer.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It would make our jobs easier.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We'd have better response times.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you go and ask for those things?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We're just going to have to pause there.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We're going to have a second round, so you're free to resume the line of questions.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we're going to hear from Council Member Wong and then Murano.

chapters.summary: Wong asks about the Quality Assurance Division's crime report auditing process. Gerber explains multiple layers: Data Integrity Unit reviews, Crime Audit Team deep dives, ICAT audits comparing 911 calls to reports, and Confidential Investigation Team for misconduct, with quarterly CAT audits per command.
chapters.title: CM Wong on crime report auditing process and quality assurance

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner Gerber, thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Previously, you testified that NYPD needs good data for resource allocation.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And my questions will be focusing on how data is collected and how data is classified.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there were audits conducted.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Between ICAT runs and the 9-11 cause.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And my question is, does the Quality Assurance Division still audit each command's crime reports?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And are those audits conducted quarterly?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yes, so if I could just explain a little bit how it works, because there actually are multiple layers of auditing that are done through the quality assurance section.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And just very briefly, so you have the DIU, the data integrity unit, and they're doing reviews.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sampling, some of it's random, some of it's targeted and focused, some of it's keyed off of various metrics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So they're doing reviews of complaints of all sorts, again, with a sort of a set methodology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So they're doing those reviews.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Separate and apart from that, the crime audit team, they are doing reviews focused in particular on looking at crime class.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: that are not major seven crime classifications, but if you're worried about misclassification, sort of where you would look, right, if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So they're doing that, and they're doing a deep dive on sampling on commands.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then we have, and they're also doing, the crime audit team also does the ICAD audits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then we also have a confidential investigation team in the quality assurance section, and that's doing investigations of alleged misconduct.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In terms of timing, the DIU work essentially is constant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's constantly happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The turnaround time from a complaint, when a complaint first comes in, if it gets flagged for DIU review, that will play out probably within three to four weeks, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, then the CAT audits, those are happening quarterly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So every command is getting reviewed in the quarter, and then that will be reported out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It plays out over the following quarter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So it takes about a quarter for that to shake out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And the radio runs, reviews are being done in each command twice a year, and that's on top of the self-inspections that are being done.

chapters.summary: Wong asks what percentage of crime reports were misclassified in 2025 and follows up on a data request from his predecessor. Gerber says they'll work with Wong's office to provide the requested data, noting the predecessor's request came days before leaving office.
chapters.title: CM Wong on audit report data and predecessor's unfulfilled request

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So let's take the quarterly CAT audit.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Do they have, for each command, do they have like a form number or a report number?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Or no, like when was the audit last completed?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Like for command, any command.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Take my present, 110.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right, so what will happen is CAT will do a sample across various types of categories of complaints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Like I said, they'll do a deep dive on each of those complaints to see if there are any misclassification issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then they'll do a report, and they'll say, here are, you know, what percentage of complaints were classified properly, if there are any that were misclassified, flagging those for the command.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, yeah, there's going to be a report.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So what percentage, say, in 2025 of those crime reports were incorrect or misclassified?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, again, it's happening across multiple units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So I can't, in other words, you have the DIU process, which is sort of ongoing, and you have the CAT work, and you have the ICAD checks, and you have the CIT work, how many of you will investigate your work?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But, Council Member, we have, you put in the letter a few days ago to us requesting various categories of data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We will, of course, work with your office to get you the various pieces that you asked for.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because my predecessor asked for these audit reports, and he didn't hear it back.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So I am following up with that.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: That is why.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I send out that letter to this morning's press release.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think he put in the request a few days before he left the council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think it was literally a matter of days before he left.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You have put in a request, sitting council member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Of course, we're going to work with you and your team, and we will get you the data that you've requested.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

chapters.summary: Wong describes constituents being turned away when trying to file police reports for stolen bikes, catalytic converters, and rims, and being told not to call 911. Gerber says these are exceptions, asks Wong to refer cases to IAB, and emphasizes most officers take reports properly.
chapters.title: CM Wong on constituents being discouraged from filing crime reports

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The reason I'm concerning is because...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: When I worked for him, we got these phone calls of people that went, call 911 and

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: were told that they're not going to take, no police report to be taken, or they went in the police precincts and they asked for a fire police report and they were turned away.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So it seemed to me, at least in my district, but it seems to be as a citywide problem that

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: these crime stats do not accurately reflect what's really happening out there because people were told they're not taking the reports or not to file a report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So a few things on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And Chair, if I may have just a few moments to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, again, this is not a new issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And are there times in which cops, officers do not take crime complaints correctly?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yes, that happens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's a relatively small number of officers, but it does occur.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We have extensive, extensive checks in place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I described to you sort of the whole auditing process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And in the commands, there are other layers as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The crime analysis sergeant, the self-inspections that happen, detective bureau follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So there are any number of things, systems in place that we have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: What you've seen under Commissioner Tisch is a tremendous focus on compliance and oversight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And frankly, to the extent, on those occasions when officers engage in misconduct, the disciplinary consequences are severe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And what I would say is, if there's ever a time when your office receives a complaint of a police officer not properly taking a crime report, please refer that to us immediately, and it will be sent to IAB immediately for investigation.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'm looking forward to see the QA order reports because, again, I have to respond to my constituents.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: They don't feel there's any safer or crime is down, and I have to answer to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I got to say, though, I got to say, we're talking about murders and shootings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Is a suggestion that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There are bodies that we're unaware of?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We're talking about overall crime data that does not accurately reflect.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: This is not talking about murders or shootings.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: This is about ordinary citizens who want to file a police report and it will turn away.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Like from stolen bikes, stolen catalytic converters, stolen rims, you know, that normally a police report will be taken, but they're not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And, sir, if...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And on occasions when that happens, right, please tell us so we can investigate and take appropriate steps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: This is very important to us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But I want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: These are the exceptions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The vast majority of police officers are doing this the right way, trying to help victims, taking proper complaint reports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we have a lot of checks in place, a lot, to catch those instances in which officers fall short.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, and I'm going to end that by we have individuals that were told that don't call 911.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You have a problem, call the police prison directly.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And then I hear from multiple people.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So those are my concerns coming from my end, which I believe the data that I've seen does not reflect these cases that I've just told you about.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Councilmember Marano.

chapters.summary: Morano expresses disappointment that Police Commissioner Tisch and a chief are not present at this important hearing. Gerber responds that Inspector Hout, as commanding officer of the Office of Crime Control Strategies, is the right person to testify on crime data.
chapters.title: CM Morano on absence of Police Commissioner and chief at hearing

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: First, I want to recognize the men and women of the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The reduction in shootings and murders that you've cited are a significant...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Accomplishment and our police officers deserve a whole lot of recognition for that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Before my questions, I do want to express some disappointment about who isn't here today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Inspector and Deputy Commissioner, I appreciate both of you appearing and this isn't a reflection on either of you personally, but we're holding a hearing about the accuracy of crime statistics and the safety of millions of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The Police Commission

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner isn't here, and neither is a chief.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I mean, I understand the commissioner can't attend every hearing, but the council and this committee has an obligation to oversee the NYPD, and I think a hearing of this importance warrants representation from the department's senior operational leadership.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm wondering if you can explain who made the decision about which NYPD officials would testify today, and why wasn't a chief or the commissioner available?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Council member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So Inspector Hout is the commanding officer of the Office of Crime Control Strategies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: He is exactly the right person to speak to crime data and crime trends in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There are other executives who do that as well, but he is certainly more than qualified for that and has an incredibly important role in that exact process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: He lives and breathes this every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The quality assurance section is part of professional standards division, which falls under me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I am responsible ultimately, I report to the police commissioner, for the auditing that I was describing earlier, and you have the right people here to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Terrific.

chapters.summary: Morano asks about NYPD strategy for intervening after a second felony assault arrest to prevent a third. Hout confirms commanding officers coordinate with DA offices on violent felony arrests, and Morano asks about measuring success of these strategies.
chapters.title: CM Morano on repeat offender intervention strategy

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Inspector, you testified that 263 individuals have each been arrested at least three times for felony assault this year.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In response to the chair, we just learned that repeat offenders are responsible for, I believe you said 20% of felony assaults.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's one out of every five felony assaults.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So my question is, if I understand the numbers correctly,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And if I don't, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Does the NYPD have a specific strategy for intervening after someone's second felony assault arrest in order to prevent a third?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do you coordinate with DAs to flag these individuals for particular attention?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Are you measuring the success of any of those strategies by the number of repeat arrests or by reductions in subsequent victimization?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: The commanding officers are in touch with the district attorney's office each time a person is arrested for a violent felony, and they're ensuring that work is together with them.

chapters.summary: Morano asks about the 580 officers cut from the budget and whether there was a written staffing assessment. Gerber says those positions were added by Mayor Adams at the end of his administration and were never banked on, noting NYPD has 2,000 more officers than two years ago.
chapters.title: CM Morano on 580 officer budget cut and staffing assessment

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Councilmember Areola asked about the 580 additional officers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I think the chair referenced that as well, that were removed from the final budget.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner, you indicated that you couldn't speculate about where those officers would have been assigned.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to speculate.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm asking about the planning that occurred before those positions were proposed.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Was there a written staffing assessment justifying the need for 580 additional officers?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Was that assessment revised when the decision was made not to hire them?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So if I may, I think if I'm...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That was 500-something additional officers, which I think Mayor Adams put in at the very end of his administration, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But he put those in, but he was also leaving, and so it was never clear that this was sort of real, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's like, for anyone to say, okay, we're going to add additional officers,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: but I'm not in a position to actually add the officers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That was not something that we were assuming was going to happen or banking on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I think to be clear, I think one very important point, right, is as compared to two years ago, right, we have 2,000 more cops, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: As compared to two years ago and now, 2,000 more police officers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we have a lot more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That 500 and something, we were never banking on that.

chapters.summary: Morano asks how NYPD attributes crime declines to its own strategies versus national trends, citing Baltimore's reductions. Gerber says NYC doesn't benchmark against other cities but notes NYC's achievement of historic lows in murders and shootings is unique given its starting point.
chapters.title: CM Morano on benchmarking NYC crime reductions against other cities

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The crime is down in New York City, right?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Crime's declining in cities across America, right?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Baltimore is one particularly striking example.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I don't mention that to diminish the accomplishments of our police officers.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to identify what's working and amplify that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Does the NYPD benchmark New York's crime reductions against comparable American cities?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And how are we doing when measured that way?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Which crime categories are improving faster than the national trend and which are improving more slowly?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So certainly in terms of the Comstat book and sort of the regular data that we're using, no, we're benchmarking it against New York City numbers, looking back, you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Year over year, five year, beginning of the Comstat era, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's how sort of we think about the data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I understand what you're asking about.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Basically what I'm trying to get is how you determine how much of New York's improvement is attributable to specific NYPD strategies.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Rather than broader national trends.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: For instance, I've heard some, I'm not saying this is accurate, but I've heard some say that a more stringent deportation policy has resulted in a national crime reduction.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm not saying that's true, but I'm just wondering, how do we know what we're doing is working if crime is down in every major city?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right, but so a few points on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I mean, one is...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And it's part of the challenge in doing this sort of analysis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying in terms of national trends, but of course, cities are different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They present different challenges, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And New York City, I would say, in many ways is actually singular.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think it's different than every other city in this country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The other thing I just want to point out is, for example,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, you see like crime declines, you see murder declines across the country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I know that's one, maybe that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In New York City, what's incredible about it, it's not just the crime decline, it's murders and shootings to historic lows.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In other words, it's one thing to say, okay, what percentage are murders declining in Baltimore or Chicago or New York City?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that's interesting, relevant, but a separate question is, okay, where was Chicago starting and where was Baltimore starting?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Where is New York starting?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The fact that we have been able to get murders down to the lowest number or shootings to the lowest number ever in terms of Comstat history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: With all the national trends, that is an incredible accomplishment.

chapters.summary: Morano cites a February 2025 example where murders were revised from 19 to 24 and rapes from 140 to 158, asking whether NYPD issues public corrections. Gerber explains crime reclassifications are normal (e.g., shooting victims dying later), all data is archived and publicly available, and no secrets exist.
chapters.title: CM Morano on crime data revision transparency and public corrections

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: One final question, if I may, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: One, finally.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Briefly, there was some skepticism expressed by several of my colleagues on the left and the right about whether or not the numbers are an accurate reflection of what's happening, right?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The council's briefing paper identifies an example from February of 2025.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The NYPD initially reported 19 murders and 140 rapes, and then those figures were subsequently revised to 24 murders and 158 rapes.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I understand that investigations evolve and legitimate revisions are necessary.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: When the department announces historic crime reductions and the underlying numbers subsequently change,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Does it ever issue a public correction or reconciliation?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And would you support publishing a monthly report showing crimes added, removed, upgraded, downgraded after those preliminary statistics are announced?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So a few different pieces of that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I want to try to answer all of them if I can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So one, I just want to take the example you gave, the murder number getting revised.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I mean, crimes get revised all the time for, not because anyone made even a mistake, but because the crime classification properly revises.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Murder is a perfect example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And this may, this is almost certainly probably what happened in the case you're describing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Someone was shot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: They are still alive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: A murder.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: A month later, three months later, the person dies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now it's a murder, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It is now going to be reclassified as a murder.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's not, no one did anything wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It was at time one, it was not a murder.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: At time two, it is a murder.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I want to give one other example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think it's really important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, someone says, hey, I lost my property on the subway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I lost my wallet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I had my credit card in there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I lost it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Okay, we take that as lost property, not a crime at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Then a month later, unauthorized credit card usage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now it's a grand larceny.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You've gone from properly classified as not a crime at all to properly classified as a major seven.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So that's normal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's what you would expect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And frankly, if there's any major police department in this country where you don't see that type of crime reclassification, that's a red flag.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's a big problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Because this is what happens in the normal course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, what we do is...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We archive all of these press releases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Everything's archived.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So to the extent, right, there's been, you know, reporting or articles about these changes, that is all based on the data that we put out there to the public, to the public, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So there's no secrets here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The reason why, like you're talking about, hey, at time one, you know, initially it was X number of murders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then later it's why number of murders, properly so, is because all of that is totally available to any member of the public, whether it's council members or journalists or academics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So all that information is out there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Murano.

chapters.summary: Feliz resumes the second round asking about felony assault victim-offender relationships. Hout reports 40.5% strangers, with smaller percentages for boyfriends, acquaintances, ex-boyfriends, and mothers, and a large 'cannot be determined' category.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz on felony assault victim relationship data

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We're gonna resume with a second round of questions.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So I wanna start by going back to the topic related to felony assaults, and then I'll move on to some questions about the data in the Bronx and also subway crime.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The felony assault, obviously a very serious crime.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What percent...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: About the felony assault, I don't know if you have this in front of you, has been first degree felony assault versus second degree felony assault.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: If you don't, I know that's very specific.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: We can get back to you on that one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: We can get back to you on that one.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Any data on the percent of felony assaults where the victim is someone that they know versus someone who's a stranger?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Random argument in the streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: So looking at the population to the victim,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: The stranger is about 40.5%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: A boyfriend is about 0.8%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
utterances.text: An acquaintance, 5.6%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - William Haut
