Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's 486 victims of this crime.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, and that's always counted into your crime statistics, yes?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's always counted into the crime statistics, absolutely, just depending on what classification, but yes.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, that's all I have for round two, and I too want to thank the NYPD for doing a job when they're seriously understaffed, and this has been a year of years for events here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Councilmember Caban, then Nurse, and then Wong.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And this looks like it'll be the final round of questions.

chapters.summary: Cabán cites the federal monitor finding specialty units like CRTs perform significantly worse on constitutional compliance than patrol officers. She asks why NYPD leans into specialty units. Gerber says specialty teams are deployed to high-crime areas and notes PST teams no longer exist.
chapters.title: CM Cabán on specialty units and constitutional violations

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Inspector, you testified several times that you're data-driven.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Very data-driven.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And you also mentioned a couple of times that part of what you...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: leave you need to be doing is you need more specialty units.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: You need to lean into your specialty units.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So, you know, the most recent report from the monitor details persistent constitutional violations, particularly from the specialized units.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: They found that the specialized units, like the CRTs, the PSTs, as examples,

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: that those units continue to perform significantly worse than regular patrol officers and that they failed to meet nearly every constitutional compliance benchmark established by the independent monitor.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So my question is, if you're data-driven and you want to lean into what works while also...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: You know, holding your folks accountable.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Why do you believe that what you need is more specialty units when your specialty units are some of the worst actors in terms of perpetrating unconstitutional stops?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yeah, Councilmember, so, so.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: No, that was for Inspector.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: No, no, no, Councilmember, I'm gonna answer your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I'm going to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And for starters, I don't think the inspector said that we need more special teams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think what he said was we surge resources, a variety of resources, specialized resources, and sometimes specialty units, yes, into high crime areas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That is 100% true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We do that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I think my question was, Inspector, why do you think we need to lean into more specialty units?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It wasn't Mr.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Gerber.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It was Inspector.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And we are picking here for the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And again, we didn't say...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: more specialty units, we said we deploy the resources, including specialty units, focusing on high crime areas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We do a spike in shootings, a spike in violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We're going to deploy resources, including at times specialty teams, to that area.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You mentioned PSTs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The PST teams no longer exist.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Well, he testified that he wanted more of that, more specialty teams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: He didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And in any event, the PST teams no longer exist, as I'm sure you know from reading the monitor reports.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But why can't the inspector speak for himself?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: He can speak for himself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Can he?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And I'm telling you, council member, you don't get to decide who answers on behalf of the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: If I ask a particular person what they thought about a thing, I would hope that that particular person would answer.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Well, except for the fact that you actually said...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It's based on his testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: He didn't say, he did not say what you said he said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: He didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay, well, Inspector, based on that information about the specialty units being some of the worst actors, what are your thoughts on

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: continuing the use of specialty units as opposed to, for example, the regular patrol officers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Councilmember, we use the specialty teams, as you know, to get guns off the street to address violence.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Since he can't answer my question, I'm going to ask a new question.

chapters.summary: Cabán asks how many times FID has substantiated misconduct for officers who killed civilians since 2014, and raises NYPD non-compliance with the 2020 PoliceStat law requiring reporting of deaths by police. Gerber says NYPD provides certain data to DCJS and offers to discuss specifics offline.
chapters.title: CM Cabán on FID misconduct data and PoliceStat law compliance

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: In terms of officer misconduct, can either of you tell me how many times the FID has substantiated misconduct of officers who killed civilians since 2014?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We certainly do not have that data here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We're certainly, we can get back to you in terms of that data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I will say, I will say that certainly I know of instances where FID finds that use of force by officers was not within guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That definitely happens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I want to ask my last question.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I will wait for you guys to send the answer on the murdered civilians.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So on...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Actually, now I want to ask about the police stat law, that 2020 New York State legislation.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The police stat law, the 2020 state legislation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So that requires the police department to report on the number of people killed by police and number of people who die in police custody.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And in the six years since the passage of the police stat law, the NYPD has not reported the number of deaths to the state, and it's been out of compliance with the law.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So why is NYP out of compliance with this law, and when do you plan to correct this and get into compliance?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, Councilmember, I am generally aware of the law, and we certainly provide data to DCJS in connection with that law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, to the extent there are, if you are falling short in certain ways, I'm actually, maybe we can talk offline so I can understand better what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We 100% provide certain data sets to DCJS in connection with that statute.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay, well then we probably should connect because the information

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: here is that you guys are not in compliance with that law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, and to the extent there's a question about any one particular data set or giving some and not all, happy to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I just want to be clear, as a writ large, we have reporting obligations and we certainly provide certain data sets to DCJS in connection.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Right, and writ large, you have lots of reporting obligations.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: One of them is to be in compliance with the police stat law passed by the state in 2020, and you currently are not in compliance.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So if you could follow up with why you have not been in compliance with that particular law and when you plan to get into compliance, that's the information I'm hoping for.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you and thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I see Councilmember Nurse stepped out, so we're going to go back with Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Wong asks about the Transit District 20 captain transferred for allegedly encouraging falsification of crime reports. Gerber confirms it's a pending disciplinary matter under investigation, and agrees to provide audit data on the transit district's crime reports.
chapters.title: CM Wong on Transit District 20 captain falsification investigation

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: This question pertains to Transit District 20's captain.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: On March 2025, a captain who headed Transit District 20 in Jamaica was transferred for allegedly encouraging the falsification of crime reports to downplay serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My question is, yes or no answer, is there investigation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, was it complete?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The matter is pending.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's a pending disciplinary matter.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, so this is still ongoing until...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Will he be disciplined as far as you know or that's...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, it's a pending disciplinary matter.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But a news report on his transfer last March did say that the department confirmed it has audited the transit district's crime reports.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'd like to request that you share this audit report with the office.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Can we get that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Well, again, you asked for a variety of a number of different data sets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And, again, we're going to work with your office to get the data that you requested.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yes, but this is specifically to Transit District 20's captain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So just to be clear, and to the extent you're asking for information about, you know, audit numbers, complaints to review, that sort of thing, we will get you that information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I just want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: To the extent you're asking for, I'm not sure that you are, but if you're asking for information that goes to a particular ongoing disciplinary matter, right, I want to be careful about that, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Literally, it's a pending matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we would not be, to the extent you're asking for anything that goes to, like, a pending matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We might not be able to provide that, but I do think we can definitely provide to you, again, if you're asking about, you know, data on numbers audited, error rate, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But on this case, this is about his alleged conduct of falsifying crime reports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And again, if you're asking for...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Number of complaints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: reviewed or errors found in connection with a particular precinct or transit district, we can accommodate that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I just want to be clear, again, I'm not sure we disagree, I just want to be clear that to the extent there's a request that goes to a pending disciplinary matter, that involves all sorts of other issues and we want to be careful about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But in terms of the data you're requesting, I think we can make that work.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Wong asks about complaint report finalization timelines and constituent complaints about slow 911 response times. Gerber says reports must be finalized within 24 hours with chief of department follow-up, and reiterates that all crime data is publicly available with extensive auditing.
chapters.title: CM Wong on complaint report finalization and 911 response times

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My second question is, I have time left, on reports finalized that's late.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Are complaint reports still required to be finalized within 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And what if they're late?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: They cannot do it.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What happens?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Well, I mean, what's going to happen is if there's a– every day the chief of department's office is getting data on this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So they're going to– but basically what's going to happen is if there is a complaint report that has not been finalized within 24 hours, there's going to be follow-up from the chief of department's office

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: essentially through the chain of command to that command saying, hey, you have a complaint here that has not been finalized within 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You got to finalize it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Let's get it done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And then it gets done.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You see, based upon what I heard today that, oh, there's now two borough commands in the Bronx, you know, and why do we need that?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The crime is down.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You know, this is why I'm confused here.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And then...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: As I see it, my overall...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: reaction from the constituent is that when they call 911, it takes a very long time for the police officers to respond.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And it just tells me that we don't have enough police officers.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And what I'm hearing is that, oh, we have plenty of police officers graduated, and it's clearly not enough when you compare it to the people leaving.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So what I'm trying to see is to get an accurate set of data to show that it's taking a long time for police officers to respond to a scene, or they just do not respond at all.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And this is why I'm asking about all this data, because it doesn't seem to me that...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Well, what's being published is accurately reflecting what's really happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Well, again, I'm not sure what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, all the data that you're talking about here is data that we have shared with the public that reflects crime revisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, normal course crime revisions, what you would expect to see normal course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It also reflects extensive, just wide-ranging oversight and redundancies built in to catch mistakes when they happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And again, on the rare occasions when you have misconduct, and you referenced a pending matter, to have aggressive investigation and, when appropriate, very, very serious discipline.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, well, thank you, and I look forward to reports that you can provide to me on Transit District 20.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Captain's case.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Wong.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks about recidivism rates across other major crimes beyond felony assault. Gerber says they don't have the data available but will pull it for the committee.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz on recidivism across crime categories

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Some few final questions on some of the topics that we talked about earlier.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So you mentioned that recidivism has been playing a big role, about a 20% role on the felony assaults.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What role has that been playing on the other major crimes?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We have that data.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Is that something that stands out?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So I don't know that we have that here, but certainly we can pull some of that data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We'll pull data for you, Chair, and we'll be able to follow up.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks whether specific weapon types stand out in felony assaults, such as stabbings or slashings. Gerber says what stands out is the volume of domestic violence (40%) and assaults on police/public employees (combined ~50%), rather than specific weapon types.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz on felony assault weapon types and patterns

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: On the issue of felony assaults, are there any specific types of assaults that stand out?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: For example, stabbings, slashings, or using a knife versus other dangerous instruments or anything that stands out from the felony assaults?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So what stands out, as I said earlier, was the domestic violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's about 40%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And if you combine our domestic violence and our assaults on police officers and other public service employees, that's about 50% of our felony assault.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So that does stick out for sure.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Anything about those incidents, though, that stands out?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: For example, using a knife versus using, I don't know, any weapon.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know using a dangerous instrument is part of the rule.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: What sticks out is really the volume.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That's there we have.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks about rape increases (up 3.2%) and the impact of the expanded definition. Gerber explains that combining rape and criminal sexual act numbers shows essentially flat trends from 2019, with about 25% of this year's reported rapes occurring in prior years, and credits increased reporting from survivor outreach.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz on rape statistics and expanded definition impact

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We haven't talked much about the rapes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They're up by 3.2% this year.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know it has been mentioned before that the definition was expanded so more incidents are covered.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How much of this increase would you say is due to the expanded definition?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So if you're looking at a larger time, we talked a number of times about going back to 2019, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sort of pre-pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: If you look at the 2019 numbers and look at the numbers, say, for, you know, 2026, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Almost all of...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The definition of rape expanded, as you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Things that previously would have been charged.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: as criminal sexual act now get charged as rape.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so if you take the aggregate of the rape numbers and the criminal sexual act numbers, right, that will account for sort of how that gets reallocated in light of the change in the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's really flat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: There has not really been

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: comparing, looking at it in that light and taking into account the change in the law, and so the reallocation of charges between rape and criminal sexual act, you don't really see

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: any material change, certainly no increase really from 2019 to now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Now, you know, year over year, we do see a small, there's a small increase in rapes, reported rapes this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The last two months were both down, actually, but rapes are slightly up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I think about 25% of that, roughly, is from prior years, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's a 25% number, I think.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's a substantial portion of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: The rape's reported this year, but the rape happened actually last year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And, you know, this is a crime where there is a longstanding concern about underreporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And the department has really made a priority to do everything in our power so that survivors will be comfortable coming forward and telling their stories.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: and making that as easy as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And the inspector spoke about this earlier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So to the extent you have, so if we're doing that the right way, what you would expect to see is some increase in reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Not that the number of rapes necessarily has actually increased, but rapes that were not being reported before now are being reported.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And so, you know, that I think is at least part of the story here and why you see the slight uptick.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: It's because we're really, we're doing everything we can to enable and help survivors to come forward.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks about hate crime numbers and trends. Gerber reports that over 50% of confirmed hate crimes are anti-Jewish, a striking trend since October 7, 2023, fluctuating between 50-60% of all hate crimes despite Jews being roughly 10% of NYC's population.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz on hate crime statistics and anti-Jewish trends

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, and two final questions.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So on the issue of hate crimes, you know, rapes, hate crimes, and there's just a lot of crimes that, you know, the police department obviously plays a big role, but there's much more that needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Obviously, public safety is a shared responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: On the issue of hate crimes, I know education also helps.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But just wondering, can you talk to us about the numbers related to hate crimes there?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Up compared to last year, anything that stands out about those numbers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: These are the confirmed numbers, right?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Any common theme that we see when it comes to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Yeah, so, I mean, look, the theme that we have, and this is not new, but it continues, is that over 50% of hate crimes are anti-Jewish, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Which is striking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, it's not new to this year, but if you, you know, let's say roughly 10% of New Yorkers are Jewish, but over 50%

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: of hate crimes, confirmed hate crimes, are anti-Jewish in nature, anti-Semitic in nature.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That is striking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: That is striking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, it's not new.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: This is a trend we've seen really now for a few years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: I would say certainly post-October 7th of 2023.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: For the past several years, the confirmed anti-Jewish hate crimes has fluctuated, I'd say roughly between 50 and 60 percent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Of hate crimes in this city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And that is a really, really striking, striking number.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, and very final question for today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Does the NYPD...

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, so we'll go briefly with Councilmember Wong, and then I'll ask one final question.

chapters.summary: Wong asks whether NYPD has data on cases where people were discouraged from filing reports. Gerber says they'll try to pull that data and asks Wong to refer any specific cases to IAB for immediate investigation.
chapters.title: CM Wong on data for discouraged crime reports

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Sorry, I left out.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Final question.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What happens if someone wanted to file a report and was discouraged from doing so?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So we certainly can try to pull data on that for you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And again, if you have...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: A report of that, if someone says, if you or your office learn about a situation like that, please notify us right away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Whether it's, and there are, because that will get investigated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So please, we want to hear from you on that.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks whether increased headcount could help bring down felony assault numbers. Gerber says in a vacuum more officers would help, but acknowledges budgetary constraints and emphasizes current success with existing staffing.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz on NYPD headcount and crime reduction potential

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Final question.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Does the NYPD believe that an increased headcount can play a role in helping bring specific numbers down?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: For example, the felony assaults, which are obviously concerning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: So, again, I just want to go back to what I said before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You know, if you're asking us, if you ask any police department, if you're asking us in a vacuum, you know, as between more cops and fewer cops, do we want more cops?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Sure, of course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But we're not here in a vacuum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: We do understand the budgetary constraints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: And, you know, we are having tremendous, tremendous success with the resources that we have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: You've heard that from the inspector from the beginning of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: In terms of murders and shootings and shooting victims being at historic lows, and we've been able to accomplish that with the number of cops that we have now.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Right, but would additional police officers allow us to be able to give some focus to the felony assaults?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Again, if in a vacuum,

utterances.text: We don't live in a vacuum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But if we were, if you have more cops, can you deploy those officers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: Of course that's true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Gerber
utterances.text: But again, we do understand the budgetary restraints here.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, sounds good.

chapters.summary: Feliz closes the NYPD testimony portion, thanking officers for their work, noting progress on murders, shootings, burglaries, and robberies, while acknowledging remaining challenges in felony assaults, grand larceny auto, and other categories compared to pre-pandemic levels.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz closing remarks on progress and remaining challenges

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, so I think that concludes this part of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I want to thank you all for your time.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz

utterances.text: Progress on murders, shootings, burglaries, and robberies are also at near historic lows.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Felony assaults stand out the most, but also other grand larceny involving a vehicle and many others.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So you have to afford to working together on that.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And look forward to having this conversation before the end of every year, talking about what's going well and also areas that need attention.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And yeah, thank you.

chapters.summary: Matthew Brawith of the Legal Aid Society Community Justice Unit, raised in the Bronx, testifies that broken windows policing doesn't work, citing 72% of arrests resolved with dismissal or ACD in 2025. He advocates for violence disruptors, community programs like Save Our Streets, and youth investment over policing.
chapters.title: Matthew Brawith (Legal Aid Society) testifies on community investments over policing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: It's good now?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: My name is Matthew Brawith, and I'm a community organizer with the Legal Aid Society Community Justice Unit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: I was born and raised in the Bronx, specifically Mitchell Houses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: My connection to this work is deeply personal, starting as back as 1990 when I lost my father to gun violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: That experience shaped my commitment to creating safe communities for young people and families like mine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Broken windows policing has never worked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Changing the name to quality of life doesn't change its ineffectiveness and abusive practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: More arrests have never meant more safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: In 2025, almost 72% of all arrests, including felonies, was resolved with a dismissal or ACD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Cops don't make me feel safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Prevention before crisis does.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: That means violence disruptors, outreach workers, credible and reliable community members, love, communication, stable housing, nutrition, pro-social activities for our kids, and most importantly, equality and keeping it real with our community members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: You heard us tell you many times why cops aren't the solution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: So today I will tell you what is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: The DYCD Bronx Spring Break Takeover at YMCA and East 229th Street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: The Bronx Uptown is an example of what works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Hundreds of youth community members from across the Bronx came together in a safe, welcoming space, trying to enjoy music, dance, get much-needed, valuable community resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: If you want to prevent violence, we have to recreate more safe places where young people and families can come together, build relationships, have fun, enjoy normal activities without the risk of being criminalized by NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Everyone deserves this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Young people should not feel that walking out their homes and meeting up with friends comes with the risk of being watched, profiled, and abused.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Taylor Murphy, founder of the Shoshana Chicken Murphy Foundation, acts before crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: He's doing what it takes to reduce violence and make our streets safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: He gives voices to the voiceless, black men that people label as high risk, and works with them as part of the solution to achieving safety and change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Save Our Streets is another prime example of our solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Consistency, compassion, chances to create change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Youth programs and community organizations are doing this work to make our community safer every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: I love my city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: More specifically, I love the Bronx, and I want to feel safe in my home, and I want to allow my son to hang out with his friends without the risk of being hurt due to community violence or NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: My family is safer when you invest in the Bronx, invest in our youth, invest in our community organizations already doing the work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Make prevention a priority, not an afterthought.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Give our young people opportunities before they become citizens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: and give our communities the resources to prevent violence before it happens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: I appreciate y'all.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And now Gina Mitchell.

chapters.summary: Gina Mitchell of Brooklyn Defender Services testifies that crime declines reflect community investments, not policing. She raises concerns about NYPD's racially biased surveillance practices, $1 billion in military-grade technology, custodial arrests for low-level charges, and violations of Criminal Procedure Law 15020 requiring appearance tickets.
chapters.title: Gina Mitchell (Brooklyn Defender Services) testifies on surveillance and low-level arrests

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: My name is Gina Mitchell, and I'm the attorney in charge of law reform and policy at Brooklyn Defender Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: Firstly, thank you to the Committee on Public Safety and to you, Chair Feliz, for inviting us to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: As we've heard many times this afternoon, over the past year, New York City has experienced decreasing rates of crime due in large part to investments in community resources and services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: We know that strong resource communities are best able to address the root causes of inequality, conflict and violence which drive much of the crime in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: Reliance on policing, surveillance and incarceration only creates a revolving door into the criminal legal system, further destabilising communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: One demonstrated success of these investments in the city is the city's crisis management system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: We have witnessed the power of credible messengers to build rapport, meet people where they are at, and help them to avoid further contact with the police and the legal system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: While crime rates have decreased, we're concerned by overemphasis on the role of NYPD and any implicit validation of NYPD's racially biased

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: and unconstitutional practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: NYPD continues to engage in stop and frisk abuses, utilizing a web of special response teams, task forces, and surveillance technology to justify a return to broken windows policing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: The NYPD has spent more than $1 billion in military-grade surveillance resources, primarily in low-income communities of colour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: This technology infringes on New Yorkers'dignity, privacy and First Amendment freedoms, while providing technical justification for disproportionate NYPD deployment to black and Latin neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: Transparency in the NYPD's use of surveillance technology is necessary for the City to have meaningful oversight of the Department's use of this technical justification for broken windows policing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: In our written testimony, we have highlighted a number of recommendations to continue to work towards community safety, but in my limited time, I will highlight just a few.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: The City should invest in interventions that have proven effective in reducing violence, including cure violence and community-based programming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: The Council continues to prioritise public health responses that support, not criminalise, people living with mental health concerns, people who use drugs and those experiencing food or housing insecurity,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: building upon the progress of the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: aggressive caucuses crisis to care initiative.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: Additionally, the council should investigate NYPD's misuse of custodial arrests for low-level charges, including quality of life policing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: This practice contributes to people with medical conditions and mental health issues entering precincts and jails in which the NYPD is not equipped to provide needed medical attention,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: and at least five New Yorkers have died in NYPD custody in 2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: And I'll just end with this final point that NYPD routinely violates criminal procedure law section 15020,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: which requires them, with limited exceptions, to issue appearance tickets in lieu of arresting individuals charged with violations, infractions, misdemeanors, and certain class E felonies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: And we did hear some discussion at length about the issuing of, or the arrest of people on the trains taking up two seats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: And as a public defender, I can tell you I've seen many of those cases coming through.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: Thank you for your time, and I do welcome any questions.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So one question for each of you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So the first one is for Matthew.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So you mentioned earlier resources to help bring down crime.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You know, we need opportunity, not just police resources, but all the other resources to give people opportunity, keep them busy, and et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Talk to us about some of the successes and also any lives changed.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: due to these resources.

utterances.text: I know you mentioned the YMCA.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Any stories that stand out on that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: From the YMCA or just in general from CMS?

utterances.text: In general, CMS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: And they had mentors and people that was like family that showed them, that's not blood, but that showed them the way to live and survive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: And it's not just...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Telling someone is showing them and being there when you think no one is there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: That's what matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Like within the system, people say, I work nine to five.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: After five o'clock, it's over.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: With crisis management system, it's 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: You get calls three in the morning, and they're picking up, and they're there for that person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: So it's an ongoing thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: You can't just say, I'm going to do this temporarily and think something's going to change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: It's consistency, and you've got to give people chances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: When you see black kids and you know they was, like they was talking about the statistics with murders and crime, they're not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: Distincting it from kids and adults.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: We got to know what the kids is doing because we got to help these children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: You get what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: So that's important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: So you got to give these kids chances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: They're going to be on, they say, the neighborhoods and the corners that they hang on, but they need other resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: You give them jobs and opportunities, then they're going to change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matthew Brawith
utterances.text: If you don't give them that, you don't give them no change.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Okay, good.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And also, a question for Jean.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Talk to us about the mental health issues and also the subway-related issues, people sleeping in the subways that you've come across.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: What cases stand out on that issue?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: As a public defender, many of our clients, when we meet them, are presenting with mental health issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: Often they have gone in and out of hospital settings, or they haven't been able to receive adequate support in the community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: We have seen...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gina Mitchell
utterances.text: An increase in the number of people being charged for taking up two seats on the subway.

chapters.summary: Glenn Balofsky of the 504 Dems testifies about the connection between the Department of Finance's stipulated fine program, double parking by commercial fleets, and funding for domestic violence victims. He advocates for reintroducing legislation to restore funding and improve street safety.
chapters.title: Glenn Balofsky testifies on parking program and domestic violence funding connection

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: Very nice to see you, Chairman Philez and your Sergeant of Arms and all the council members that were here today and Jumaane as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: What was a stark and very interesting part of the police department's

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: testimony was the problems we're having with domestic violence in our great city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: It's a real shanda, as we say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: It's a crime against humanity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: People hurting each other's families and children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: And what plays into this is that we know more than 30% of our school children today are homeless as well as a result.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: But what we want to bring to your attention as disabled advocates, disability advocates, part of the 504 DEMS, is this, that the Department of Finance is taking money away

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: from individuals who are victims of crime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: Under the New York City's Department of Finance stipulated fine program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: which nearly passed under Corey because we had a super majority of 39 members on, we believe is being introduced again, 1141, 2018, under Julie's leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: And this will restore a lot of funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: To help improve the lives of victims of domestic violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: It has a direct correlation, parking and victims of domestic violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: Who would ever make that connection?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: But it's true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: And the Amazons of the world are not paying this, along with the mega fleets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: So, of course, that's a public safety issue here, because when the vehicle's double parked, nobody can see around it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: It causes tremendous issues of public safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: Bicyclist safety, disability, members of the disability community on our team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: They can't even get into the accessorized vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Glenn Balofsky
utterances.text: And so we're excited about that being reintroduced to help stop the insanity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: So I was president of the Junior Park Civic for 25 years, served on Community Board 5 in Queens for 30 years, and I chaired its public safety committees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: And I co-founded COP 104, which brought our local precinct and communities together for monthly meetings for more than 20 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: So, you know, I know our precincts, and I know how the system used to work, folks, used to work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: And I can tell you that something changed dramatically over the last maybe three or four years, and I've never seen it this bad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: My council office heard the same story over and over again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: Constituents called 911, waited an hour or longer for police, and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: they were either discouraged from filing a report or they were told it's not really a crime or nothing is going to happen anyway and detectives aren't going to investigate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: These are some of the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: excuses we got, or even the DA wouldn't prosecute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: That is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: A crime victim should never have to argue with the government just to take a report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: I repeatedly told commanding officers, take the report, please, just take it, and they said,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: Let the facts determine what happens next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: But after decades of dealing with the NYPD, what concerned me most was this no longer looked like a few isolated incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: I began hearing from people inside the department that commands were under tremendous pressure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: To keep complaint numbers down, and in some cases, classify crimes at a lower level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: And so that raised serious questions with me and my staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: And there were coordinated efforts to, you know, there was apparently a coordinated effort to keep crime numbers artificially low.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: I mean, that's what I suspected in many others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: Again, we needed to look at the facts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: So maybe it was intentional.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: Maybe nobody ever put it in writing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: But tremendous pressure came down from City Hall or one police plaza to commanders of the precincts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: And that the pressure worked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: It's way down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: Either possibility demands an investigation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: So because when the same complaints are coming from victims,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: police officers and people inside the department, and then the internal audits that could provide answers are kept from the public view, you cannot just dismiss this as a coincidence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: So I'll say it plainly, I do not trust these crime stats that we're getting today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: And this is not an attack on the rank-and-file cops.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: I've been supporting the cops for decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: I've supported our police.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: On every level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: If anything, they may be victims of the system too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: When commanders are pressured to produce lower numbers, that pressure eventually reaches the cop answering the 911 calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: So before I left office, whistleblowers raised serious concerns with me and to me about the NYPD's Quality Assurance Division audits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: I was told some audits found upwards of 70% of reports reviewed were either classified below what the facts warranted or that a required report was never taken at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: Think about what that means.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: If somebody commits a crime and no report is taken, as far as the stats are concerned, that crime never happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: So I was told the quality assurance unit was so understaffed it could not conduct broader audits and that findings like these should have been triggered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: So I commend Councilmember Phil Wong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: Oswald Feliz for continuing to pursue this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: The council should demand the audits, staffing members, levels and procedures and command findings and correct this action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: NYPD cannot publish the headline and hide the audit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: So if they refuse to turn over records that the public should see,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: I guess we should subpoena them in the council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: After more than four decades of working with our local precincts and the NYPD, I know what I saw.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: Something changed in the last three or four years, and New Yorkers deserve at least to know why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: Whether this is an intentional scheme, pressure from above, or a culture that everyone understood that the numbers had better go down, we need to get to the truth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: You cannot let the fox guard the hen house, and you cannot stand at the podium, pat yourself on the back, and tell New Yorkers crime is down while hiding the very audits that could tell us whether those numbers are worth the paper they're printed on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: So, again, thank you for waiting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the technical problems, but great hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Holden
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Robert, and thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And thank you for all the work you've done on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Is there anyone who would like to testify in person?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I don't see anyone here.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I don't see anyone online.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If yes, please use the raise hand function.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I don't see anyone else registered online, so I just want to thank everyone who has joined us today, everyone who watched, everyone who testified.

chapters.summary: Council staff confirms no further witnesses are signed up to testify and adjourns the hearing.
chapters.title: Hearing adjourned

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: This hearing is hereby adjourned.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

summary: Oversight hearing on NYPD crime statistics featuring Inspector William Hout and Deputy Commissioner Michael Gerber reporting historic lows in murders and shootings, with major crime down 6.2% year-to-date, while felony assaults and rape have increased

Council members questioned NYPD on crime reporting accuracy, repeat offender recidivism (263 individuals arrested 3+ times for felony assault), Bronx resource allocation (40% of city shootings), unconstitutional stops by specialty units, and transparency in data revisions

Public testimony included advocates from Legal Aid Society and Brooklyn Defender Services calling for community investment over policing, disability advocates linking parking enforcement to domestic violence funding, and former CM Robert Holden alleging crime stat manipulation
